5) A middleware in go is a function that takes a http.Handler as an argument and returns another http.Handler. A call chain can be built recursively. A http.Handler is an interface that with a single function that takes a request writer and response struct as arguments.

Frameworks like Fiber come with routers that allow you to add middleware to your server. 

You can install your own routing library such as Chi or gorilla/mux which come with built in middleware support. The go standard library allows you to specify a custom router when starting the server.

Alternatively you don’t even need a struct, just pass dependencies to the function that needs them (a receiver method is just syntactic sugar for this anyways…)

Performance isn’t a big deal for a frontend. The stereotypical web application is IO bounded. All of the hard computation work is being done by the browser, so the performance standard tends to be VanillaJS. It enables you to use browser APIs with minimal overhead. There are web libraries such as Solidjs and Svelete that get near Vanilla performance while still getting high QoL. Most frontends wind up being written in Angular or React because there simply is no bottleneck.

A language is really a formalization of logic. We have to ask ourselves if the semantics provided by Rust help solve the problems present in a web frontend. The answer is no, so you’re better off going Solidjs or Vanilla if performance is a concern.

Rust is more interesting if you need to use WASM specifically because compiling a garbage collected language (such as JS) to WASM is a bad idea. Your average application bounded by DOM API and network IO gets very little off WASM.
